spark.summary: An agentic CLI coding harness pairs a local ReAct tool-execution loop (Bash, file edit, grep, git) with OS-level sandboxing, AST-backed repo mapping, prompt-prefix caching, and auto-compaction to solve multi-file engineering tasks from the terminal.
spark.keyTakeaway: If model quality drifts from offline training baselines, keep the harness thin and deterministic: isolate side effects in an OS sandbox, enforce explicit permission gates on writes/exec, and preserve prompt-cache prefixes across tool iterations.
spark.byteSummary:
Unlike IDE autocomplete engines that predict a few lines around the cursor, an agentic CLI coding harness operates autonomously in a terminal ReAct (Reason-Act-Observe) loop across an entire repository. The harness mediates between a remote frontier LLM and the developer's local filesystem, exposing structured tools for ripgrep search, AST symbol inspection, targeted file patching, and bounded shell execution.

Because every tool call appends file contents and test output to the conversation, context growth is the primary latency and cost bottleneck. Production harnesses solve this by keeping the system prompt, tool schemas, and repo map immutable at the front of the prompt (achieving >80% KV/prompt-cache hit rates) and triggering automatic context compaction at ~85-90% window capacity.

Safety and recoverability are equally critical: destructive shell commands and out-of-workspace file writes pass through a policy permission gate (Allow/Ask/Deny) and execute inside OS sandboxes (macOS Seatbelt or Linux seccomp/namespaces), while shadow Git snapshots let the user roll back any multi-file edit atomically.

learningJourney.title: The Terminal ReAct Loop & Structured Tool Schemas
learningJourney.purpose: Connect LLM reasoning turns with deterministic local tool dispatch and streaming terminal rendering.

explanation.foundation: Think of **The Terminal ReAct Loop & Structured Tool Schemas** as the intuition layer for Agentic CLI Coding Harness Architecture: Connect LLM reasoning turns with deterministic local tool dispatch and streaming terminal rendering.
explanation.core: The CLI runs an event-driven loop: send messages + JSON tool schemas to the LLM, stream thinking/text deltas to an ANSI/TUI diff renderer, parse `tool_use` blocks, execute the local tool with a strict timeout, and append `tool_result` back to the message array. Bounded step limits (e.g., max 50 turns) and duplicate-call detectors prevent infinite edit-fail loops.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, the terminal react loop & structured tool schemas becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Architect Seatbelt/seccomp sandboxing, optimistic concurrency file guards, and read-only MCP subagent fan-out.

learningJourney.title: OS-Level Sandboxing & Permission Policy Gates
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent arbitrary shell execution or prompt injection from damaging the host machine.

explanation.foundation: Think of **OS-Level Sandboxing & Permission Policy Gates** as the intuition layer for Agentic CLI Coding Harness Architecture: Prevent arbitrary shell execution or prompt injection from damaging the host machine.
explanation.core: Running an LLM-generated `bash` command directly on a developer laptop risks `rm -rf`, credential exfiltration, or network leaks. A Permission Policy Engine classifies every tool call into Read-Only (auto-allow), Workspace Write (ask once or session-allow), or Dangerous Exec (explicit user confirmation), while wrapping subprocesses in macOS `sandbox-exec` (Seatbelt) or Linux `bubblewrap`/`seccomp` with read-only root and blocked outbound network by default.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, os-level sandboxing & permission policy gates becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Architect Seatbelt/seccomp sandboxing, optimistic concurrency file guards, and read-only MCP subagent fan-out.

sectionDiagram.summary: Policy gates and OS sandboxes contain untrusted commands and prompt-injected tool calls.
sectionDiagram.caption: Seatbelt and seccomp enforce filesystem and network boundaries at the kernel level.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Agentic CLI Coding Harness Architecture without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: If model quality drifts from offline training baselines, keep the harness thin and deterministic: isolate side effects in an OS sandbox, enforce explicit permission gates on writes/exec, and preserve prompt-cache prefixes across tool iterations.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: AST Repo Mapping & Targeted File Reading
learningJourney.purpose: Give the agent global codebase awareness without stuffing 100K lines into the prompt.

explanation.foundation: Reading every file in a 5,000-file repository exhausts context immediately.
explanation.core: Instead, the harness builds a compact Repo Map using Tree-sitter AST parsing + PageRank over symbol references, fitting the most central classes, function signatures, and file paths into ~2,000 tokens.
explanation.deepDive: The agent then uses `ripgrep` (`rg`) and line-range reads (`start_line..end_line`) to inspect only relevant slices.

learningJourney.title: Prompt-Prefix Caching & Deterministic Cache Alignment
learningJourney.purpose: Slash API cost and TTFT by 80% across 20-turn coding sessions.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Prompt-Prefix Caching & Deterministic Cache Alignment** as the intuition layer for Agentic CLI Coding Harness Architecture: Slash API cost and TTFT by 80% across 20-turn coding sessions.
explanation.core: A 25-turn debugging session re-sends the system prompt, tool definitions, repo map, and earlier turns on every iteration. Placing static instructions, tool schemas, and `CLAUDE.md` project rules at the exact byte-for-byte start of the prompt—with explicit `cache_control` breakpoints—lets the LLM provider serve 85%+ of input tokens from KV-prefix cache at 10x lower cost and 3x faster TTFT.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, prompt-prefix caching & deterministic cache alignment becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Architect Seatbelt/seccomp sandboxing, optimistic concurrency file guards, and read-only MCP subagent fan-out.

learningJourney.title: Auto-Compaction & Context Budget Management
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent context overflow during marathon refactoring sessions without losing critical state.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Auto-Compaction & Context Budget Management** as the intuition layer for Agentic CLI Coding Harness Architecture: Prevent context overflow during marathon refactoring sessions without losing critical state.
explanation.core: When cumulative tokens approach 85-90% of the context window, the harness triggers Auto-Compaction before the next LLM call. Old verbose `tool_result` outputs (like 500-line test logs) are pruned first; if still over budget, a fast summarizer model condenses earlier turns into a structured state brief (modified files, failing tests, architectural decisions) while keeping the last few turns verbatim.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, auto-compaction & context budget management becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Architect Seatbelt/seccomp sandboxing, optimistic concurrency file guards, and read-only MCP subagent fan-out.

learningJourney.title: Atomic Patching & Shadow Git Rollback Snapshots
learningJourney.purpose: Guarantee clean, conflict-free file edits and instant one-command undo.

explanation.foundation: Asking an LLM to rewrite an entire 800-line file wastes output tokens and risks silent deletions.
explanation.core: Instead, the `edit_file` tool requires exact search-and-replace hunks (`old_string` -> `new_string`) verified against a pre-edit file hash/mtime to prevent stale overwrites.
explanation.deepDive: Before each turn's mutations, the harness writes a lightweight shadow Git tree (`git write-tree` in a separate index) so `/undo` restores the exact workspace state atomically.

cards.detail: Reject edits if the user modified the file in their IDE concurrently.

sectionDiagram.summary: Exact hunk matching and shadow Git trees make agentic edits fast and safely reversible.
sectionDiagram.caption: Optimistic concurrency checks prevent clobbering concurrent developer edits.

learningJourney.title: Parallel Subagent Fan-Out & Headless MCP Integration
learningJourney.purpose: Delegate noisy codebase exploration to isolated subagents without polluting main context.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Parallel Subagent Fan-Out & Headless MCP Integration** as the intuition layer for Agentic CLI Coding Harness Architecture: Delegate noisy codebase exploration to isolated subagents without polluting main context.
explanation.core: When an agent needs to investigate 4 different microservices, reading 30 files in the main loop fills the context window with irrelevant code. The harness spawns isolated read-only subagents with their own fresh context windows and MCP tool servers (GitHub, Jira, Postgres schema), returning only concise 500-token findings summaries to the parent agent.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, parallel subagent fan-out & headless mcp integration becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Architect Seatbelt/seccomp sandboxing, optimistic concurrency file guards, and read-only MCP subagent fan-out.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does an agentic CLI coding harness place the system prompt, tool definitions, and AST repo map at the very beginning of the prompt without dynamic timestamps?

options.text: To keep the prompt prefix byte-for-byte identical across turns so the LLM provider's KV-prefix cache hits on 85%+ of tokens.
options.feedback: Correct! Any mutation near the start of the prompt invalidates the entire downstream KV-cache prefix.

options.text: Because Tree-sitter only parses files if timestamps are removed.
options.feedback: Tree-sitter parses local source files independently of prompt formatting.
Prompt layout has no effect on OS subprocess sandboxing.

options.text: Because JSON tool schemas cannot be parsed after turn 1.
options.feedback: Tool schemas are parsed on every turn; keeping them static is purely for prefix-cache reuse.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Prompt-prefix caching matches exact token prefixes from index 0. Keeping static instructions, schemas, and repo maps at the front saves ~80-90% of input token cost and TTFT.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the primary advantage of using exact search-and-replace hunks (`old_string` -> `new_string`) with an mtime/hash check instead of rewriting entire files?

options.text: It allows the agent to skip running unit tests.
options.feedback: Tests still need to run to verify behavior.

options.text: It cuts output token generation by 10x, prevents accidental truncation of untouched code, and detects concurrent IDE edits.
options.feedback: Correct! Targeted hunks are faster, cheaper, and safe against stale-file overwrites.

options.text: It eliminates the need for a permission gate.
options.feedback: File writes should still obey workspace permission policies.

options.text: It automatically pushes commits to GitHub.
options.feedback: Hunk edits only modify local files atomically.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Rewriting full 1,000-line files is slow, expensive, and prone to truncation. Targeted hunk patching with optimistic concurrency checks is fast and reliable.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should parallel repo-exploration subagents be restricted to read-only tools by default?

options.text: To prevent concurrent write-write race conditions and conflicting file edits across parallel subagents.
options.feedback: Correct! Parallel subagents mutating the same working tree would cause race conditions and corrupt files.

options.text: Because read-only tools do not consume any LLM tokens.
options.feedback: Subagents still consume LLM tokens for their own context.

options.text: Because ripgrep cannot run inside a sandbox.
options.feedback: ripgrep is a read-only tool and runs cleanly inside sandboxes.

options.text: To disable prompt caching on the parent agent.
options.feedback: Subagents have isolated contexts and do not affect parent prompt caching.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Restricting parallel exploration subagents to read-only tools avoids filesystem races while keeping noisy file reads out of the parent agent's context.

beginner.summary: Understand how terminal coding agents like Claude Code read your codebase, run tests safely, and edit files step by step.
beginner.keyTakeaway: If model quality drifts from offline training baselines, keep the harness thin and deterministic: isolate side effects in an OS sandbox, enforce explicit permission gates on writes/exec, and preserve prompt-cache prefixes across tool iterations.
beginner.byteSummary:
Terminal coding agents work inside a simple loop: they read your request, inspect relevant files using fast search tools like ripgrep, propose a small edit, and run tests to check their work.

To keep your laptop safe, risky shell commands ask for your permission first and run inside an OS sandbox, while a hidden Git snapshot lets you undo any multi-file change in one command.

intermediate.summary: Build an agentic CLI harness with Tree-sitter AST repo maps, prefix-cache prompt layout, 90% auto-compaction, and hunk patching.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: If model quality drifts from offline training baselines, keep the harness thin and deterministic: isolate side effects in an OS sandbox, enforce explicit permission gates on writes/exec, and preserve prompt-cache prefixes across tool iterations.
intermediate.byteSummary:
Production CLI harnesses balance autonomy with token efficiency and safety. A Tree-sitter + PageRank repo map gives global codebase context in ~2K tokens, while ripgrep and line-bounded reads fetch only needed slices.

Placing static instructions, tool schemas, and the repo map at the front of the prompt unlocks >85% provider prompt-cache hits. When context hits 85-90%, two-stage compaction prunes stale tool logs before summarizing older turns, and exact hunk patches with shadow Git snapshots ensure atomic rollback.

advanced.summary: Architect Seatbelt/seccomp sandboxing, optimistic concurrency file guards, and read-only MCP subagent fan-out.
advanced.keyTakeaway: If model quality drifts from offline training baselines, keep the harness thin and deterministic: isolate side effects in an OS sandbox, enforce explicit permission gates on writes/exec, and preserve prompt-cache prefixes across tool iterations.
advanced.byteSummary:
At enterprise scale, CLI harnesses enforce kernel-level isolation using macOS Seatbelt or Linux bubblewrap/seccomp, blocking credential paths (~/.ssh, ~/.aws) and unapproved network egress even under prompt injection.

To scale across million-line monorepos, the parent agent delegates multi-service investigations to isolated read-only subagents connected via MCP servers, receiving concise file:line citations without polluting its primary reasoning context.
